newsitem.title: UK: Commodity markets dull after volatile moves.
newsitem.headline: Commodity markets dull after volatile moves.

text.p: Global commodity markets took a breather on Friday, settling in narrow price bands after some volatile roller-coaster rides earlier in the week.
Precious and industrial metals stabilised after hitting fresh lows earlier in the week.
Cocoa prices reversed a downward drift after data showed higher European chocolate consumption but volume was scant.
Business was lacklustre in general as commodity markets found it difficult to capture investors' attention as world stock markets kept roaring to new record highs.
The Standard and Poors Index of 500 leading firms shattered the 700 mark, while the Dow industrial average also soared.
Trading in commodites was more muted.
Aluminium and most of the rest of the base metals settled at lower levels carved out earlier in the week.
Aluminium, the second most-traded industrial metal, ended the week above 2-1/4 year lows hit on Thursday, but the rise was not very convincing.
Metal for delivery in three months finished trading on the London Metal Exchange (LME) up $5 from Thursday at $1,357 per tonne but still well below the week's opening level of $1,416.
The flagship metal, copper, recovered from a dip below $1,900 on Thursday but ended the week slightly easier.
Earlier in the week, tin slid to 16-month lows and lead to the weakest values in seven months but both recovered slightly by the close on Friday.
Metals traders, producers and consumers gather in London starting Monday for LME week, the biggest industry gathering of the year.
The precious metals markets also stabilised after gold dived under the $380 benchmark on Tuesday, touching the lowest levels in 18 months.
By Friday, however, prices were back where they started the week -- nervously straddling the $380 area.
Dealers and analysts debated whether the market had bottomed out or was just resting before taking another stab at the downside.
Cocoa prices made a U-turn after a week of declines when data shook the market showing that consumption was on the rise.
Grind figures -- tracing the amount of cocoa beans ground for chocolate and other uses -- surprised traders by shooting up in the Netherlands and Britain.
Prices on London's benchmark March futures contract rose to 1,000 sterling in London before gains were pared. It ended seven sterling higher at 992.
Coffee continued its uptrend with good buying from speculators after inventory figures earlier this week dropped to a 12-year low.
Prices ended in London with a $24 gain at $1,519 per tonne.
Grains in Chicago were mostly softer amid forecasts for good seedling and harvesting weather.
